section_1_unit_metadata.essay_thesis_one_sentence: The Heideggerian Ruf des Gewissens (BT §§54-60), heard as a silent ontological-temporal interruption that summons Dasein to authentic being-toward-itself, operates structurally as primordial epideictic rhetoric — a showing-forth (epideixis) of the heart of human existence — thereby grounding Aristotle's epideictic genus (Rhetoric I.3, I.9) in fundamental ontology and disclosing what Heidegger himself, despite his violent appropriation of the Rhetoric in 1924 and Being and Time, never quite admitted: that rhetoric (and not poetry alone) has ontological-disclosive status.

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: [Opening — no heading]
argumentative_moves: Quotes Gadamer's testimony from 'Heidegger's Ways' (Stanley trans., SUNY 1994, 31-32) on what it was like to listen to Heidegger lecture on Aristotle in early-1920s Freiburg/Marburg — Heidegger's 'critical and de(con)structive' powers, his freeing of the original text from scholastic distortion, the centrality of phronesis (practical wisdom) in the 1923 NE seminar.

Foregrounds Gadamer's framing of Heidegger's 'violent appropriation' of Aristotle as itself analogous to the call of conscience in BT — both 'first make the Dasein in human beings visible in its ontological and temporal event-structure.'

Glosses 'violence of hermeneutic phenomenology' as Heidegger's 'doing violence' to interpretive complacency, exposing 'tranquillized obviousness' of everyday interpretations; the 'interruption' is meant to 'incite specific feelings of anxiety and joy.'
Links the Ruf des Gewissens to Heidegger's pedagogical practice — Heidegger's textual violence is itself an act of conscience awakening students to phronesis lost in scholastic prejudice.

Quotes the BT 178 passage (the volume's most-cited single quote): 'this work of Aristotle [the Rhetoric] must be taken as the first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of Being with one another' — frames the entire chapter as building on Heidegger's positive reception.

Establishes Hyde's twofold rhetorical operation: (i) further confirming rhetoric's 'ontological status' along Heidegger's lines, and (ii) 'sounding such a call' — i.e. the chapter is itself epideictic, performing what it argues for.

Opens the central thread: Aristotle's analysis of the emotions (pathē) as oriented to communal bond/identification with the audience, and the special role of the enthymeme as connecting emotion-rhetoric to the call of conscience.
Stakes the bridge thesis: 'the call of conscience operates as a primordial form of rhetorical (that is, epideictic) discourse.'
section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_register: philosophical-introductory, with deliberate self-positioning as itself epideictic

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: I. EMOTION AND RHETORIC
argumentative_moves: Frames Plato's Gorgias / Phaedrus / Sophist anti-rhetoric position (rhetoric caters to emotion and inhibits noēsis/epistēmē) and the Phaedrus admission that rhetoric may serve truth (Socrates speaking through the personification, Phaedrus 260d-e).

Pivots to Aristotle's two clarifications: (1) emotional character constitutes a person's spirited potential for judging the true/just/virtuous; (2) rhetoric is dynamis (capacity, faculty, power) — 'the counterpart of Dialectic' (Rhet. 1354a1) — not a technē in the manipulative sense.
Cites Rhet. II thesis (1377b24): the orator must 'put his hearers into the right frame of mind' so that their world-orientation matches the orator's truth-claim.

Quotes Heidegger's GA 18 (163) gloss in German: 'Es muß bei der Vorgabe anderes in Hinsicht gestellt werden... die jeweilige Lage der Dinge und die Art and Weise, wie man selbst zur Sache steht' — and 'Er bedarf des Verständnisses der Möglichkeiten der Stimmung, um sie in der rechten Weise zu wecken und zu lenken' (also from GA 18).
Argues that the orator's competence is not 'mere communicative device' for chatter (Gerede) but is 'something good' that makes rhetoric more than the publicness of idle talk.

Reads BT §27 on das Man / averageness (BT 165, 'In this averageness with which [publicness] prescribes...') as the negative pole, and BT §27 (BT 167, 'publicness belongs to Dasein's positive constitution') as the positive — Hyde insists Heidegger's account of publicness has both poles.
Cites Dreyfus (1991) commentary: 'the source of the intelligibility of the world is the average public practices through which alone there can be any understanding at all.'

Quotes Heidegger's gloss of doxa from GA 18 (149): 'Die doxa ist die eigentliche Entdecktheit des Miteinanderseins-in-der-Welt' — doxa as 'authentic discoveredness of being-with-one-another in the world.' Establishes the doxa-Mitsein bridge.

Detailed analysis of Aristotle's anger (orgē): personal rather than at-an-object; Rhet. 1378a32-34 (the 'conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous slight'), Rhet. 1378b3-5 ('the angry man is aiming at what he can attain, and the belief that you will attain your aim is pleasant'), Rhet. 1380b5 ('time puts an end to anger').

Reads anger as a temporally-modifying emotion: anger collapses imagined future revenge into present immediacy; Hyde interprets this as a 'perceptual restructuring of a person's existential temporality and spatiality' — explicitly translating Aristotle into the Heideggerian existentialia of temporality/spatiality.

Anger-fear interrelation: Rhet. 1382a30 (slight by powerful other), 1382b20, 1383a15-20 — 'fear forces the realization that what was heretofore perceived to be remote is actually close at hand.' Anger thus 'modifies the lived space of our everyday being-with-others.'

Anger-pity-fear triangulation via identification (Rhet. 1382b26, 1385b15-34, 1386a1-3, 1386b5-10) — pity arises through identification with another's threatened circumstances; anger and pity cooperate in modifying lived time/space.

Concludes Section I: Aristotle's pathē-analysis exhibits 'a systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of Being with one another' (BT 178) and Heidegger continues this in BT's analysis of fear-vs-anxiety (temporal/spatial 'workings' of fear vs. more 'primordial' workings of anxiety; BT 179-182, 228-235); the 'in-depth analysis of the ways in which [the pathē] are interconnected in their foundations' (BT 178) is what Heidegger admittedly omits but Hyde recovers.
section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_register: philological-exegetical (anchoring Aristotle's pathē in Heidegger's existential-ontological vocabulary)

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: II. THE ENTHYMEME
argumentative_moves: Rhet. I.2 enthymeme as 'syllogism' (1356b3) but a special one: 'not constructed out of any haphazard material... but out of materials that call for discussion... [and] debate' (1357a35-39).

Rhet. I.2 1357a1-4: enthymeme handles 'such matters as we deliberate upon without arts or systems to guide us, in the hearing of persons [untrained thinkers] who cannot take in at a glance a complicated argument.'

Rhet. I.2 1357a15-20: enthymeme proceeds with 'few propositions, fewer often than those which make up the normal syllogism. For if any of these propositions is a familiar fact, there is no need even to mention it; the hearer adds it himself.' Audience supplies the missing premise.
Cites Rhet. I.2 1377b24: enthymeme intends to put the audience 'into the right frame of mind.'

Reads Rhet. III contradiction (1418a11-14: avoid enthymeme when rousing feeling) as resolved by reading enthymeme via two senses of enthymeisthai: 'taking something to heart' (emotional take-up) AND 'giving consideration' (cognitive take-up).

Cites Heidegger's GA 18 (95-107) on theoretical-as-derivative-of-practical: 'any purely theoretical assessment of some subject matter is derivative of one's more practical, everyday, and emotional involvement with things and with others.'

Reads Heidegger's gloss on enthymeme as 'sich etwas zu Herzen nehmen' (GA 18 [128]) — to take something to heart — as the primary, audience-cooperative function; this is the enthymeme as ground/soil of the logos (den Boden des logos selbst, GA 18 [169]).
Cites P. Christopher Smith (1998, Hermeneutics of Original Argument): Heidegger 'radically redirects' Aristotle's enthymeme to favor the ambiguous reading toward 'taking to heart.'
Cites Henry Johnstone Jr. (1978) and the Hyde 1969 mid-century debate on rhetoric/emotion to historicize the move.

Bridges to Section III by claiming: the enthymeme — like the call of conscience — invites concerned, embodied take-up; the orator who heeds Heidegger's call advances 'an ontological appreciation of the orator's art.'
section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_register: technical-rhetorical-philosophical (the most rhetorical-theoretical section of the essay)

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: III. THE CALL OF CONSCIENCE
argumentative_moves: Recapitulates: 'the orator must understand the possibilities of moods [die pathē] in order to rouse them and guide them in a right and just way' (in der rechten Weise) — restated as collaborative deliberation requiring the formation of common interest.

Quotes Aristotle Politics 1281b1-6 (the famous 'Many' passage): 'Each of them by himself may not be of a good quality; but when they all come together it is possible that they may surpass — collectively and as a body, although not individually — the quality of the few best.'
Quotes NE VI 1141b8-11 on phronesis: 'practical wisdom is concerned with things human and things about which it is possible to deliberate.'

Etymological move: 'phronesis' rooted in 'phren' (the heart); collaborative deliberation as syn-eidesis (Greek 'knowing together') / con-scientia (Latin 'knowing together'). Conscience IS this togetherness-of-knowing.

Cites Taminiaux (1992, Heidegger and the Project of Fundamental Ontology, 141): from manuscripts of Heidegger's Sophist / Philebus / SS 1926 lectures, Heidegger said 'phronesis is Gewissen [Conscience] set in motion which makes an action transparent [durchsichtig].' Confirmed by Gadamer 1976 (Philosophical Hermeneutics, 201) on the 1923 NE seminar.

Pivots to BT's call of conscience proper: Ruf des Gewissens 'comes forth originally in the way in which our temporal and spatial existence (Dasein's Being-in-the-world) confronts us with a fundamental challenge calling for a response' — the contingency of the future, the 'not yet,' the task of 'creating a meaningful existence.'

Stakes the not-a-human-invention claim: 'we did not create the ontological (temporal/spatial) structure of existence — the way it opens us to the contingency of the future and thereby, within this openness, gives us a place to be toward all that stands before us.' Conscience precedes ethics: 'the call of conscience is always already operating before the specific ethical prescriptions and prohibitions of [moral] language.'

Quotes BT 318 (§56): 'The call dispenses with any kind of utterance. It does not put itself into words at all. . . . Conscience discourses solely and constantly in the mode of keeping silent.' The call is silent.

Quotes Heidegger on language as 'saying' (Sage) — 'To speak means to say, which means to show and to let [something] be seen. It means to communicate and, correspondingly, to listen, to submit oneself to a claim addressed to oneself and to comply and respond to it.' (footnoted to Zollikon Seminars, p. 215, but echoes On the Way to Language).

Quotes BT 316 (§55): the call is 'an abrupt arousal' that interrupts complacent everyday involvements; conformity to averageness 'belongs to the inauthentic state of our Being-with-others' because it 'relieves us from the burden of explicitly facing the challenge' of resoluteness.

BT 342 (§57): 'the anxiety of conscience' — anxiety and conscience 'go hand in hand.' Anxiety arises with disruption (illness, crisis) that 'exposes us to the contingency and uncertainty inherent in our temporal existence.'

Quotes BT 232, 317-335: 'Anxiety makes manifest in Dasein its Being towards its ownmost potentiality-for-Being, a potentiality which it always is and that is spoken of directly with the saying of the call of conscience.'

Concludes Section III: the call's 'ground and soil' is precisely what enthymematic reasoning (Section II) and pathē-analysis (Section I) operate on — the ontological ground for Aristotelian rhetoric is BT's existential-temporal openness.
section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_register: BT-exegetical (the most direct exegesis of BT §§54-60 in the volume)

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: IV. EPIDEICTIC DISCOURSE
section_2_hierarchical_outline.ocr_status_for_section_opening: PDF p. 100 (book p. 94) is rotated 180 degrees. Inverted reading recovers: Hyde's prior euthanasia-debate work; Cope citation defining epideictic; classical genus distinctions.
argumentative_moves: Opens by referring to Hyde's prior monograph (Hyde 2001, The Call of Conscience: Heidegger and Levinas, Rhetoric and the Euthanasia Debate, U of S. Carolina Press) on the moral discourse of the euthanasia debate. The euthanasia debate 'is quite capable of reaching down to the heart of human being' — rhetoric as both deconstructive and reconstructive in life-and-death cases.

Cites E. M. Cope (An Introduction to Aristotle's Rhetoric, 1867, p. 121): epideictic is the 'demonstrative,' 'showy,' 'ostentatious' rhetoric, contrasted with deliberative and forensic; Cope's etymological note that epideictic includes both encomium and invective ('praise of a man's good qualities').
Aristotle Rhetoric I.3 framework: three genres — sumbouleutikon (deliberative), dikanikon (judicial), epideiktikon (epideictic/display).
Aristotle Rhetoric I.9 framework: epideictic loci concern aretē (excellence/virtue) — the orator praises or blames moral excellence in a person.

Reads p. 95: epideictic as 'a beholding and a showing-forth (epideixis) of what is and as a competence for acknowledging others whom the orator desires to instruct as he or she gains and maintains their interests.' Epideixis = showing-forth.
Argues: 'in the euthanasia debate one finds epideictic rhetoric revealing what might be termed the most original epideictic event there is to be witnessed and taken to heart: the call of conscience.'

Crucial qualifying caveat (p. 95): 'one cannot make this claim by simply appealing to Aristotle, for the essential connection here between the call of conscience and epideictic rhetoric, and it is Heidegger, not Aristotle, who directs us toward an ontological understanding of the first of these two phenomena.' Aristotle has the eulogy / 'eine Lobrede' (GA 18 [125]) but not the ontological grasp.
Cites GA 18 (104, 123, 169) for Heidegger's emphasis 'how rhetoric (like the call of conscience) demands a hearing from those whom the orator would move with his discourse.'

Stakes the central bridge thesis (p. 95): 'Still, violent appropriation of the Aristotelian text is not violent enough when it comes to revealing how the saying of the call of conscience has something fundamentally rhetorical about it: conscience calls; it appeals to us most forcefully by way of an emotion (anxiety) that transforms time and space, opens us to the openness of our own existence, and thereby challenges us to think and act for the purpose of creating a meaningful existence... The call of conscience, which lies at the heart of human being, is a showing-forth (epideixis) of this heart, a rhetorical revelation par excellence, whereby a call for concerned thought and decisive action is announced.'

p. 96 candor: Heidegger 'does not relate the call of conscience and epideictic discourse' explicitly — Heidegger describes the call as 'a rhetorical interruption, but merely as an interruption that... calls one's existence into question and beckons one toward taking a needed course of action.'

p. 96 difference between epideixis and poiesis: Heidegger's later 'call of Being itself' is associated with poiesis (Letter on Humanism; Question Concerning Technology, 10-11; Poetry, Language, Thought, 62-74) rather than epideictic showing-forth. Hyde flags this as a missed connection: 'What I have suggested above regarding the epideictic and thus rhetorical nature of the call of conscience is certainly meant to question this omission.'
section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_register: argumentatively climactic — the bridge thesis stated as such

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: V. CONCLUSION: WHERE ART THOU, RHETORIC?
section_2_hierarchical_outline.ocr_alert_correction: The original unit metadata listed only 4 Roman sections (I-IV). The actual essay has 5 — V is 'CONCLUSION: WHERE ART THOU, RHETORIC?' starting on book p. 97. This is a Phase 2 finding correcting the Phase 0 audit.
argumentative_moves: Opens with counterfactual: had Heidegger appreciated rhetoric's connection to 'the heart of human being,' he might have responded more 'heartfeltly' to the Nazi turn and the Holocaust. Quotes Heidegger 1949 (in Wolin, The Politics of Being, 168): 'Agriculture is today a motorized food industry, in essence the same as the manufacture of corpses in gas chambers and extermination camps... the same as the blockade and starvation of countries, the same as the manufacture of atomic bombs.' Hyde calls this 'morally and rhetorically inappropriate.'
Cites Jeremiah 24:7 ('I will give them a heart to know Me') as the Old Testament-conscience parallel.

Quotes Gadamer (Truth and Method 2nd rev. ed., xxxviii): 'What man needs is not just the persistent posing of ultimate questions [for example, the meaning and truth of Being], but the sense of what is feasible, what is possible, what is correct, here and now. The philosopher, of all people, must, I think, be aware of the tension between what he claims to achieve and the reality in which he finds himself.'

Pivots to Cicero as the Roman recovery of conscience-rhetoric. Cites De oratore 3.16.61 (the 'absurd and unprofitable severance between the tongue and the brain'); De oratore 3.14.55 (orators sans virtue would be 'putting weapons into the hands of madmen'); De officiis 1.7.22 (philosophy as essential to the well-equipped orator); Orator 33.118; De officiis 1.6.19 (active life vs. study); De oratore 1.8.32 (the orator's moral function — to 'bring help to the suppliant, to raise up those who are cast down').

Reads Cicero as practitioner of vita activa whose rhetoric ('art of eloquence,' oratio) equips knowledge for civic action — closes the loop on the chapter's epideictic-conscience bridge by showing that Cicero's tradition keeps rhetoric joined to the heart.

p. 99 closing claim: 'as Heidegger developed his philosophy, a sincere concern for the truth and goodness of rhetoric disappeared from view... such a disappearance has never been a healthy sign for rhetoric.'

Final emphasis: Heidegger's later trajectory toward the call of Being / poetry, while productive, leaves the orator's art disappearing — 'a sincere concern for the truth and goodness of rhetoric disappeared from view.' Cicero's critique of philosophy ('absurd and unprofitable severance between the tongue and the brain') 'is well worth remembering when journeying on Heidegger's path of thought that leads away from rhetoric and the call of conscience and toward poetry and the call of Being.'
section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_register: epideictic-political — Hyde performs precisely the rhetoric he theorizes (a praise/blame, showing-forth of Heidegger's missed opportunity)

section_3_key_concepts.name: Call of Conscience
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: An ontological-temporal phenomenon disclosing itself in Dasein's confrontation with the contingency of the future, the 'not yet,' and the task of constituting a meaningful existence; the call dispenses with utterance and discourses 'solely and constantly in the mode of keeping silent' (BT 318); always already operating before the specific ethical prescriptions of moral language; revealed paradigmatically in moments of 'abrupt arousal' (BT 316) and anxiety (BT 342). Hyde's central thesis: the call IS a primordial form of epideictic — a showing-forth (epideixis) of the heart of human existence.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Epideictic Rhetoric
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotle's third rhetorical genre (Rhet. I.3) alongside deliberative (sumbouleutikon) and judicial (dikanikon); the rhetoric of praise and blame whose loci are the virtues (Rhet. I.9). Hyde follows Cope (1867 p. 121) in glossing the term as 'demonstrative,' 'showy,' 'ostentatious' — but radicalizes the gloss ontologically: epideictic is the showing-forth (epideixis) of what is, especially of the existential structure of the heart. The call of conscience is THE primordial epideictic event.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Pathē / Emotion as Cognitive-Existential
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotelian pathē are not raw feelings but constituents of the subject's potential to judge truth, justice, and virtue (Rhet. II); they orient the audience and modify temporal-spatial existence (cf. Rhet. 1378a32-34 on anger; 1382a30 on fear; 1386a1-3 on pity). Hyde aligns pathē with Heidegger's Stimmung and reads BT's analyses of fear (BT 179-182) and anxiety (BT 228-235, 342) as continuing the Aristotelian project. Crucial: pathē are 'rooted first and foremost in what book 2 of the Rhetoric is all about: the emotional fabric of a person's existence' or 'the ground and soil of the logos' (GA 18 [169], den Boden des logos selbst).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Enthymeme
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Rhetorical syllogism (Rhet. 1356b3) operating with few propositions wherein the audience supplies the missing premise (Rhet. 1357a15-20). Hyde reads enthymeisthai dually as (i) cognitive 'giving consideration' AND (ii) emotional 'taking something to heart' (sich etwas zu Herzen nehmen, GA 18 [128]) — citing Heidegger's appropriation. The enthymeme thereby grounds collaborative deliberation in the soil/ground of the logos.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Phronesis
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotle's NE VI virtue concerning 'things human and things about which it is possible to deliberate' (NE 1141b8-11). Hyde activates the etymological link phronesis-phrēn ('the heart') and the syn-eidesis (Greek) / con-scientia (Latin) etymology: collaborative deliberation = knowing-together. Crucially cites Taminiaux (1992 Heidegger and Project of Fundamental Ontology, p. 141): Heidegger said 'phronesis is Gewissen [Conscience] set in motion which makes an action transparent (durchsichtig).' This is the strongest textual warrant for the BT-conscience / Aristotle-phronesis identity.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Anxiety
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: BT §40 + §57 phenomenon — the mood that 'goes hand in hand' with the call of conscience (BT 342). Anxiety arises through disruption (illness, crisis) that exposes Dasein to the contingency and uncertainty of temporal existence. Hyde treats it as the ontologically privileged emotion that 'transforms time and space' (p. 95) and is 'spoken of directly with the saying of the call of conscience' (BT 232, 317-335).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Anger
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotelian pathos (Rhet. 1378a30-1380b5) presented as Hyde's primary illustration of how pathē modify temporal/spatial existence: anger collapses imagined future revenge into present immediacy (Rhet. 1378b3-5 'pleasant to imagine attaining'); time dissolves anger (Rhet. 1380b5 'time puts an end to anger'); slights modify lived space because the person becomes 'close at hand' (Rhet. 1382a30, 1382b20, 1383a15-20).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Pity
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotelian pathos (Rhet. 1382b26, 1385b15-34, 1386a1-3, 1386b5-10) bound to anger and fear via identification: A pities C when A can identify with C's threatened circumstances; identification (cf. Burke 1969) marks a 'lack of remoteness' that modifies lived space.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Hermeneutic Violence
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's pedagogical practice in 1923-24 of 'doing violence' to scholastic prejudice in his readings of Aristotle. Gadamer (Heidegger's Ways 33) calls this 'the most original experience of Dasein.' Hyde reads Heidegger's textual violence as itself analogous to the call of conscience — both interrupt complacent everyday interpretations to summon attention. Hyde explicitly performs his own violence in turn ('I also intend to sound such a call, and with a bit of violence, too,' p. 83).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Doxa as Authentic Discoveredness
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Quoting Heidegger GA 18 [149]: 'Die doxa ist die eigentliche Entdecktheit des Miteinanderseins-in-der-Welt' (doxa is the authentic discoveredness of being-with-one-another in the world). Hyde uses this to soften the negative pole of das Man and ground epideictic in the public space of doxa.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Showing-forth / Saying
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's recurrent gloss of language as a 'showing' (Aufzeigen — already in BT, cf. Hyde's citation Zollikon Seminars 215, 'To speak means to say, which means to show and to let [something] be seen') and the later Sage. Hyde aligns this Heideggerian 'showing-forth' with Aristotle's epideixis (the act of epideictic) — it is the same structural operation in two registers (existential-ontological / rhetorical-classical).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Publicness / Idle Talk
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: BT §27 / §35 phenomenon. Hyde insists Heidegger has BOTH a negative pole ('mass-like, crowd-like, herd-like' — BT 165) AND a positive pole (BT 167: 'publicness belongs to Dasein's positive constitution'). The positive pole authorizes the rhetorical work of the orator who modifies public moods.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Resoluteness
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: BT §60 — the existential structure of authentic potentiality-for-Being. The call of conscience summons resoluteness; ethics emerges as 'the responsibility of affirming our freedom through resolute choice.'

section_3_key_concepts.name: Three Genres of Rhetoric
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Rhet. I.3 typology. Hyde uses it conventionally but emphasizes the epideictic genus as the ontologically privileged one (the genus that shows-forth what is the case rather than what should be done or what was done). This is where Hyde's reading diverges from BCAP unit U-FP3a — see VT10.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Call of Being
section_3_key_concepts.german_form: Anruf des Seins (cf. Letter on Humanism)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's later thinking — the 'call of Being itself' associated with poiesis (poetry as 'bringing-forth' of truth) rather than with epideixis (rhetoric as 'showing-forth'). Hyde flags the difference and makes it the chapter's productive pivot: Heidegger never asks 'what is the difference between epideixis and poiesis?' — that omission is what Hyde's chapter contests. Cited as note 23 (BT 49-58, 314, 310-325; On the Way to Language 57-136) and note 31 (QCT 10-11, PLT 62-74).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Considerateness / Forbearance
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: BT 159 phenomena (note 43, also Hyde's Call of Conscience 57-64). Heidegger's terms for 'authentic response from non-Arian Others' — the rhetorical-ethical dispositions Nazism could not accommodate. Hyde uses these to politicize the call-conscience-rhetoric bridge.

section_4_main_positions.claim: The Heideggerian Ruf des Gewissens (BT §§54-60) operates structurally as primordial epideictic rhetoric: a silent, ontologically-prior showing-forth (epideixis) of the heart of human existence, summoning Dasein to the contingency of the future and to resolute responsibility-for-self.
premises: (P1a) Aristotle's pathē are constituents of judgment, not noise (Rhet. II), and Heidegger affirms this in BT 178 + GA 18.
(P1b) The enthymeme functions audience-cooperatively as 'taking something to heart' (sich etwas zu Herzen nehmen, GA 18 [128]) — the rhetorical operation has an emotional ground.
(P1c) Heidegger's call of conscience is silent (BT 318) and is heard as a temporal-spatial interruption that opens Dasein to its ownmost potentiality-for-being (BT 232, 316, 317-335).
(P1d) Aristotle's epideictic genus (Rhet. I.3, I.9; Cope 1867) has 'showing-forth' (epideixis) as its primary act and aretē as its content.

(P1e) The structural identity of (P1c) and (P1d) — both are showings-forth of moral excellence in temporal-spatial situations — warrants reading the call of conscience AS primordial-ontological epideictic.
targets: Scholastic readings of Aristotle's Rhetoric Heidegger himself targeted
Heidegger's own omission: he 'never attempts to relate the call of conscience and epideictic discourse' (p. 96)

section_4_main_positions.claim: Aristotle's analysis of pathē (Rhet. II.1-11) provides Heidegger with the rhetorical-existential vocabulary that BT operationalizes as the analyses of fear (§30), anxiety (§40), and conscience (§§54-60); the SS 1924 lectures (GA 18) are the conceptual hinge.
premises: (P2a) Heidegger's BT 178 statement that the Rhetoric is 'the first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of Being with one another' is a primary-text endorsement.
(P2b) Heidegger's GA 18 glosses (cited 122f, 128, 137, 146f, 149, 163, 165, 169) translate Aristotle's pathē-vocabulary into the existential register (Stimmung, Befindlichkeit, Lage, Sorge).
(P2c) BT 178-182 + 228-235 + 342 develop fear-vs-anxiety in the temporal/spatial register — continuous with Aristotle's analysis of how anger/fear/pity modify lived time and space.
targets: readings of Heidegger that ignore his Aristotelian-rhetorical formation

section_4_main_positions.claim: Phronesis IS Gewissen (Conscience) 'set in motion' that makes an action transparent (durchsichtig) — Heidegger said this in his SS 1924-26 lectures, per Taminiaux (1992) and Gadamer (1976), and the etymological chain phronesis-phrēn (heart) / syn-eidesis / con-scientia confirms it.
premises: (P3a) Aristotle NE VI: phronesis is concerned with what is deliberable (1141b8-11).
(P3b) The Greek phrēn = heart; syn-eidesis = knowing-together; Latin con-scientia = same.

(P3c) Taminiaux 1992 (Heidegger and Project of Fundamental Ontology, p. 141) reports Heidegger said this in a manuscript of the Sophist / Philebus / Basic Concepts of Ancient Philosophy lectures (24/25/26).
(P3d) Gadamer 1976 (Philosophical Hermeneutics, p. 201) recalls Heidegger's 1923 NE seminar making the same point.
targets: readings that separate Heideggerian conscience from Aristotelian phronesis

section_4_main_positions.claim: Anger, fear, and pity are not psychological epiphenomena but operations that 'restructure existential temporality and spatiality' — they bring the not-yet of the future close, dilate or contract the lived space, and constitute identification (cf. Burke 1969). This is precisely what Heidegger's existential-temporal analysis of moods enacts.
premises: (P4a) Rhet. 1378a32-34 + 1378b3-5 + 1380b5: anger collapses future revenge into present pleasure and dissolves with time.
(P4b) Rhet. 1382a30, 1382b20, 1383a15-20: fear closes spatial distance from threat.
(P4c) Rhet. 1382b26, 1386a1-3, 1386b5-10: pity arises through identification = lack of remoteness.
(P4d) BT 179-182, 228-235: Heidegger distinguishes the temporal/spatial workings of fear from the more 'primordial' workings of anxiety — same conceptual operation.
targets: reductive readings of Aristotle's pathē as raw feelings

section_4_main_positions.claim: The enthymeme's audience-completion function (Rhet. 1357a15-20) bridges to Heidegger's 'sich etwas zu Herzen nehmen' (GA 18 [128]) — taking-to-heart names the emotional/cognitive dual register; enthymeisthai means both 'giving consideration' AND 'taking to heart.' This dual reading dissolves the apparent Rhet. III contradiction (1418a11-14: avoid enthymeme when rousing feeling).
premises: (P5b) Rhet. 1418a11-14 (apparent contradiction with feeling-rousing).
(P5c) GA 18 [95-107]: theoretical-as-derivative-of-practical (Heidegger's foundational claim).
(P5d) GA 18 [128]: sich etwas zu Herzen nehmen — taking-to-heart.
(P5e) GA 18 [169]: enthymeme as 'ground and soil of the logos' (den Boden des logos selbst).
(P5f) Smith 1998 Hermeneutics of Original Argument 27-29: Heidegger 'radically redirects' enthymeme.
targets: Smith's gloss further specified; readings that resolve Rhet. III by dismissing enthymeme's emotional role

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger's later 'call of Being' is associated with poiesis (poetry, bringing-forth) rather than with epideixis (rhetoric, showing-forth), and the absence of explicit thinking on the difference between epideixis and poiesis is a productive omission Hyde's chapter contests. Heidegger's later turn from rhetoric to poetry leaves rhetoric's ontological status under-acknowledged.
premises: (P6a) BT 49-58, 314, 310-325 — early-Heidegger emphasis (note 23).
(P6b) Letter on Humanism (Capuzzi/Gray 210) — later Heidegger.
(P6c) On the Way to Language (Hertz 57-136); QCT (Lovitt 10-11); PLT (Hofstadter 62-74) — call of Being / poiesis.
(P6d) 'Heidegger... never considers this question as he moves from a concern with rhetoric in his early philosophy to a concern with poetry in his later philosophy' (p. 96).
targets: the trajectory of Heidegger's later thought; readings that endorse Heidegger's late turn without contesting it rhetorically

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger's failure to acknowledge rhetoric's ontological status correlates with the moral-rhetorical inappropriateness of his 1949 'agriculture/extermination camp' equation, his Nazi turn, and his 1930s-40s silence — the absence of conscience-rhetoric leaves a vacuum Cicero's tradition (Republic / De oratore / Orator / De officiis) would have filled.
premises: (P7a) Heidegger 1949 quote (cited via Wolin 1990 Politics of Being, 168): the equation of agriculture with extermination is 'morally and rhetorically inappropriate.'
(P7b) Cicero De oratore 3.16.61: 'absurd and unprofitable severance between the tongue and the brain.'
(P7c) Cicero De oratore 3.14.55: orators sans virtue would be 'putting weapons into the hands of madmen.'
(P7d) De oratore 1.8.32: orator's moral function is 'to bring help to the suppliant, to raise up those who are cast down.'
(P7e) Gadamer T&M xxxviii: philosopher must be aware of the tension between ultimate-question pursuit and feasibility/here-and-now reality.
targets: readings of Heidegger's late thought that disconnect it from his political failure
the disappearance of rhetoric's ontological status from continental philosophy

section_4_main_positions.claim: Hyde's chapter is itself epideictic — it performs the rhetoric it theorizes. The chapter sounds a call of conscience to readers (especially philosophers and rhetoricians) toward Heidegger's missed opportunity, and it does so 'with a bit of violence' (p. 83) following Heidegger's own pedagogical model.
premises: (P8a) Gadamer's testimony (Heidegger's Ways 33): Heidegger's textual violence makes Dasein visible; the same operation is what Hyde aims to perform on Heidegger.
(P8b) p. 83: 'I also intend to sound such a call, and with a bit of violence, too.'
(P8c) The 'showing-forth' of Heidegger's missed opportunity is structurally an epideictic event.
targets: a reading of the chapter as merely descriptive scholarship rather than performative epideictic

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Hyde acknowledges that Heidegger 'never attempts to relate the call of conscience and epideictic discourse' (p. 96) and 'never considers' the difference between epideixis and poiesis as he moves from rhetoric (early) to poetry (later). Hyde's bridge thesis (P1) is therefore an extrapolation from Heidegger's framework that Heidegger himself did not make. This is not a contradiction in Hyde's argument but a calibrated declared productive ambiguity: the chapter advances a reading 'with a bit of violence' (p. 83) — analogous to Heidegger's own violent appropriation of Aristotle.

Tension between Hyde's reading of conscience as silent (BT 318) — non-linguistic in any utterance sense — and the chapter's claim that conscience is rhetorical (i.e., a form of discourse). Hyde resolves this through the Sage / Aufzeigen / showing-forth reading: language at the ontological level is showing-and-letting-be-seen, not utterance, hence the silent call IS rhetorical without being verbal.

VT5 (per phase0-overview) — pathos as cognitive resource vs. ontological substrate. Hyde treats pathē as deliberate orator-deployable rhetorical resources (the orator must 'put his hearers into the right frame of mind') AND simultaneously as ontologically primordial existentialia (Stimmung/Befindlichkeit). Gross treats pathos as 'the very substance in which propositional thought finds its objects and motivation' (Intro p. 4) — pre-cognitive ontological substrate. The two readings are compatible (Hyde's epideictic-conscience claim SUPPORTS Gross's broader pathos-as-substrate claim) but operate at different registers: Hyde keeps the orator's intentional structure intact while Gross dissolves the orator into pre-cognitive disposition. Hyde's orator-position is closer to Aristotle's NE phronimos; Gross's is closer to Heidegger's pre-thematic Befindlichkeit. The chapter explicitly does both — pathē are 'rooted in the emotional fabric of a person's existence' AND deployed by the orator.

VT10 (per phase0-overview) — Hyde's epideictic emphasis vs. BCAP unit U-FP3a's deliberative emphasis. Heidegger's GA 18 §§13-14 (which BCAP indexes as U-FP3a) treats rhetoric primarily as deliberative (sumbouleutikon) — the rhetorical situation is one of practical deliberation (Beratung, krisis) about future action. Hyde imports the Aristotelian distinction (Rhet. I.3) and emphasizes the THIRD genre (epideiktikon) as the one that captures the conscience phenomenon. This is productive tension: Heidegger himself does not foreground epideictic in GA 18 (Hyde concedes p. 95: 'it is Heidegger, not Aristotle, who directs us toward an ontological understanding' — but Heidegger 'admits' epideictic only briefly, GA 18 [125] as 'eine Lobrede'). Hyde's reading thus extends Heidegger via Aristotle's typology while remaining textually constrained by Heidegger's actual emphases.

Hyde aligns broadly with HR-01-GROSS, HR-02-GADAMER, HR-05-STRUEVER on the SS-1924-as-formative-for-BT thesis (continuity), but his epideictic emphasis distinguishes him: Gross's pathos genealogy is more Stoic-Lutheran (Roman compromise → Affektenlehre), Struever's Alltäglichkeit reading is more biological-temporal (Aristotle's life-science neighborhood), Kisiel's protopolitical reading is more political (Arendtian afterlife). Hyde's register is most distinctively rhetorical-epideictic. [INTERP-low] Within the volume, Hyde's chapter is the most directly textually-grounded in BT §§54-60 specifically.

Hyde's continuity thesis (rhetoric carries through into BT) is in direct opposition to HR-07-POGGELER's restriction thesis (rhetoric is a circumscribed, ultimately abandoned moment). Hyde acknowledges Heidegger's later turn from rhetoric to poetry (P6) but reads it as the chapter's productive critical pivot — 'a sincere concern for the truth and goodness of rhetoric disappeared from view' (p. 99). Pöggeler reads the same trajectory as decisive abandonment.

Hyde acknowledges (p. 96, note 29 cite Kisiel) that Heidegger's gravitation toward HEARING (rather than speaking) 'risks losing the active involvement of the speaker in the rhetorical situation.' This is a real internal tension in Hyde's chapter: if conscience is silent and Dasein hears the call, where is the orator? Hyde's resolution: the chapter ITSELF is epideictic (P8) — Hyde is the orator, sounding a call to readers — but the call-of-conscience phenomenon proper is hearer-side.

[INTERP-low] BT pipeline unit BT-D2-U2 (§§54-60) treats Gewissen primarily within Heidegger's existentialia framework (attestation/guilt/resoluteness); the rhetorical-genealogy reading is not foregrounded. Hyde's reading retroactively ASSIGNS rhetorical structure to BT phenomena that BT itself does not name as rhetoric. Phase 4 cross-pipeline question: does BT pipeline's analysis of §§54-60 require revision (or supplementation) to incorporate Hyde's epideictic reading? The answer is likely 'supplementation, not revision' — the existentialia analysis stands but Hyde adds a structural-rhetorical layer.

Section V's political move (Heidegger's 1933, the 1949 'agriculture/extermination' equation, the missed Cicero-recovery) sits structurally apart from Sections I-IV's textual analysis. The connection (P7) is: missing rhetoric's ontological status correlates with moral failure. But Hyde does not fully argue that the textual claim entails the political claim; the move is more rhetorical than logical (which is appropriate to an epideictic chapter that performs what it argues for).

section_10_local_graph_edges.note: Hyde's central thesis: the call of conscience IS the ontological-primordial form of epideictic — a silent showing-forth (epideixis) of the heart of human existence.

Hyde reads BT §55 (the 'character of conscience as a call', H.289 + 316 + 318) as operationalizing Aristotle's epideictic genus (Rhet. I.3, 1358b1ff) in the existential register — the call IS the existential-ontological form of epideictic.
BT 318: 'Conscience discourses solely and constantly in the mode of keeping silent.' The silent call IS the showing-forth (epideixis / Aufzeigen / Sage). Silence as ontological show.
Heidegger's GA 18 [163] (the Stimmung/Lage gloss) presupposes Aristotle's Rhet. 1377b24 ('put hearers into the right frame of mind'). Same operation translated into the existentialia register.

Hyde aligns Aristotle's pathē with Heidegger's Stimmung — pathē constitute spirited potential to judge (truth/justice/virtue), Stimmung is the ontological mood-structure that constitutes Befindlichkeit.

Per Taminiaux 1992 / Gadamer 1976: Heidegger said phronesis is Gewissen 'set in motion' that makes an action 'transparent' (durchsichtig). Etymological warrant: phronesis-phrēn (heart) / syn-eidesis / con-scientia.

Aristotle's analysis of orgē (Rhet. 1378b3-5, 1380b5) — anger collapses imagined future revenge into present immediacy and dissolves with time — is read by Hyde as a perceptual restructuring of existential temporality (BT temporality framework).
Pity (eleos, Rhet. 1382b26, 1386a1-3) modifies lived space via identification ('lack of remoteness'); Hyde reads this as an operationalization of BT's existential-spatial categories.

Hyde reads enthymeisthai dually — 'taking something to heart' (sich etwas zu Herzen nehmen, GA 18 [128]) AND 'giving consideration' (cognitive). The dual structure operationalizes the call of conscience: the call sounds in the audience-completion of the enthymeme.

GA 18 [169]: enthymematic-rhetorical practice is 'den Boden des logos selbst' (the ground and soil of the logos itself). Heidegger explicitly grounds logos in rhetoric here — Hyde's strongest GA 18 anchor.

Hyde's epideictic-conscience thesis SUPPORTS Gross's broader pathos-as-substrate thesis (Gross frames pathos as 'the very substance in which propositional thought finds its objects and motivation'). Hyde specifies the rhetorical register; Gross frames the genealogical-ontological register. The two are compatible at the level of register-distinction (per VT5).

Hyde's reading of pathē as restructuring existential temporality/spatiality SUPPORTS Struever's broader Alltäglichkeit-as-timefulness thesis. Both align Aristotle's rhetorical-life-science vocabulary with BT's temporal analysis.

Hyde's continuity-with-late-critical-pivot thesis CONTRASTS WITH Pöggeler's restriction thesis. Hyde acknowledges Heidegger's later turn from rhetoric to poetry but reads it as missed opportunity; Pöggeler reads it as decisive abandonment. The volume opens with Gross-Hyde-Struever-Kisiel arguing continuity and closes with Pöggeler arguing restriction.

Hyde's epideictic emphasis REFINES the BCAP unit U-FP3a reading of GA 18 §§13-14 (which centers deliberative rhetoric). Hyde imports Aristotle's epideictic-deliberative-judicial typology (Rhet. I.3) and isolates the third genre as the one capturing the conscience phenomenon. This is productive cross-pipeline tension VT10.

BT 342 (anxiety of conscience) presupposes BT 232 ('Anxiety makes manifest in Dasein its Being towards its ownmost potentiality-for-Being'). Anxiety and conscience 'go hand in hand' (Hyde p. 93) — the call of conscience is the existential-rhetorical content of the anxiety-disclosure.

Cicero's tradition (De oratore, Orator, De officiis) supports Hyde's claim that Heidegger's later turn away from rhetoric correlates with moral-rhetorical failure. The Roman recovery shows what Heidegger missed.

Hyde follows Gadamer (Heidegger's Ways 31-32, 33) in reading Heidegger as the most powerful historicizing reader of Aristotle in the 20th century — the 'violent appropriation' frees the original text. Aristotle is rendered 'visible in his ontological and temporal event-structure' through Heidegger.

Late Heidegger's call of Being is associated with poiesis (bringing-forth) rather than epideixis (showing-forth). Hyde flags this as a productive omission: Heidegger 'never considers' the difference between epideixis and poiesis — and the chapter's bridge thesis contests this omission.

Per Gadamer (Heidegger's Ways 33): Heidegger's 'violent appropriation' of Aristotle is itself analogous to the call of conscience — both interrupt complacent everyday interpretations to summon attention. Hyde's chapter performs the same operation on Heidegger's omissions.
Per GA 18 [149]: 'Die doxa ist die eigentliche Entdecktheit des Miteinanderseins-in-der-Welt.' Doxa as the authentic discoveredness of being-with-one-another — the ontological-rhetorical bridge.
Hyde's phronesis = Gewissen identity (P3) is corroborated by Gadamer's testimony in the volume's Ch 2 interview about the 1923 NE seminar. Direct intra-volume cross-citation.

Aristotle NE VI 1141b8-11 (phronesis as deliberation about the human-deliberable) is operationalized by Heidegger's existentialia of conscience (BT §55, H.289). The phronesis-Gewissen identity is the operational link.

The chapter's own epideictic performance (P8) exemplifies its central thesis (P1): Hyde sounds a call of conscience to readers about Heidegger's missed opportunity. The chapter does what it argues for — a self-referential rhetorical structure.

Plato's Gorgias-Phaedrus-Sophist anti-rhetoric position is contrasted with Aristotle's pro-rhetoric clarification (rhetoric as dynamis, pathē as constituents of judgment). Heidegger reads Aristotle in this regard, not Plato.
